Dram
DRAM
noun
From the Greek drachme through the Latin drachma and Old French drame, a small weight and the coin struck to it; the Authorized Version uses dram to render the Hebrew darkemon and adarkon, the Persian daric of gold.

Biblical Definition

A dram is a small gold coin of the Persian empire, weighed rather than counted, which the Authorized Version sets in the returning-exile books and in David’s last assembly. It is a word of the treasury, and every time it appears it appears in a list of what men gave willingly toward the house of God. David, having set the pattern with his own substance, records what the princes offered for the temple his son would build: gold, and silver, and brass, and iron, and among them “ten thousand drams” (1Ch 29:7). Ezra records the same generosity on the far side of the captivity, when a poor and diminished people gave “after their ability” threescore and one thousand drams of gold to the work (Ezr 2:69), and Nehemiah numbers the Tirshatha’s thousand and the fathers’ twenty thousand (Neh 7:70–72). Small coins, told in heaps, given by many hands. The doctrine of the dram is the doctrine David spoke over the heap: that we are able to offer willingly only because all things come of God, and that what we lay down is of His own already given us (1Ch 29:14). The dram therefore never establishes a claim upon God. It is a returning, not a purchase; a confession that the Giver owns the gift and the giver both, and that the house of God is built by grace flowing back to its source.

Webster 1828 Definition

A small weight and coin; in Scripture the Persian gold daric, reckoned by tens of thousands among the freewill offerings for the house of God.

expand to see more

DRAM, n. [Gr. drachme; L. drachma.] Among the ancients, a small weight and a silver coin.

In apothecaries’ weight, the eighth part of an ounce; in avoirdupois, the sixteenth part.

In the Scriptures, a coin of gold, the Persian daric, rendered dram in Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah.

Hence, any small quantity; a little; as much as one may drink at once.

The word marks the smallness of the single piece against the greatness of the sum gathered.

Key Scripture

1Ch 29:7 — "And gave for the service of the house of God of gold five thousand talents and ten thousand drams, and of silver ten thousand talents, and of brass eighteen thousand talents, and one hundred thousand talents of iron."

Ezr 2:69 — "They gave after their ability unto the treasure of the work threescore and one thousand drams of gold, and five thousand pound of silver, and one hundred priests' garments."

Neh 7:70 — "And some of the chief of the fathers gave unto the work. The Tirshatha gave to the treasure a thousand drams of gold, fifty basons, five hundred and thirty priests' garments."

Neh 7:72 — "And that which the rest of the people gave was twenty thousand drams of gold, and two thousand pound of silver, and threescore and seven priests' garments."

Modern Corruption

The prosperity gospel takes the drams laid down for the house of God and turns them into seed money — a transaction with heaven rather than a returning of what heaven gave.

expand to see more

The live corruption is the prosperity gospel, which has made the offering plate a place of exchange. Its preachers — the name-it-and-claim-it line running from Kenyon and Hagin down to the television ministries of our own day — teach that money given is money sown, and that God is bound by a law of return to multiply it back to the giver in kind. Paul named that error before it had its modern name, warning of men “supposing that gain is godliness” (1Ti 6:5), and adding that the love of money is the root of all evil, which some coveting have erred from the faith and pierced themselves through with many sorrows. The dram texts destroy the scheme at its foundation. David’s princes did not give in order to receive; they gave because they had already received, and David’s doxology over the heap confessed that all things come of God and that of His own they had given Him. Where giving is a lever upon God it has ceased to be worship and become commerce, and the poor are the ones bled by it.

Recover the willingness and the smallness. Ezra’s returned remnant gave “after their ability” — the measure is not the sum but the ability, which is why the widow’s two mites outweighed the rich men’s abundance in the Lord’s own reckoning. A dram is a small coin; sixty-one thousand of them are a temple treasury. The church is not built by a few great patrons but by many ordinary hands laying down small things cheerfully, and the God who owns the gold of every hill is pleased to receive from His people what was already His. Give as a debtor to grace, not as a creditor to God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Persian gold daric; the small coin whose heaps built the house of God out of freely given substance.

expand to see more

Dram — Greek drachme, Latin drachma, Old French drame: a weight and the coin struck to it.

Hebrew darkemon / adarkon, the Persian daric of gold (Ezr 2:69; Neh 7:70–72; 1Ch 29:7).

Every biblical occurrence stands in a list of gifts toward the temple or its rebuilding.

Distinguished from the talent, a great weight; the dram is the small piece.

David’s rule over the whole heap: of thine own have we given thee (1Ch 29:14).

Usage

"Drams are counted in tens of thousands: the sum is large because the givers were many, not because each was rich."

"Read every dram text with David’s confession attached — the gift returns to its Owner."

"Ezra’s “after their ability” is the standard by which giving is measured, not the printed total."
